title: Car trapped in floodwater
quickSummary: Stay calm. Lower or break a window before water pressure seals the doors.
steps: 1. Stay as calm as you can. Do not panic and shout, which wastes oxygen.
2. TURN THE ENGINE OFF immediately so a short circuit or water intake does not drag the car deeper.
3. UNBUCKLE YOUR SEAT BELT, and unbuckle children and other passengers.
4. OPEN A WINDOW AT ONCE. Before water rises past the middle of the glass, the electrics may still work for a few dozen seconds.
5. If a power window is stuck, strike a SIDE window at the four CORNERS with a rescue hammer. Windshields are much harder to break.
6. If you have no hammer, pull out a headrest and jam the two metal posts into the window seam, then lever hard.
7. Wait until pressure equalizes. A deeply submerged door will not open. When water reaches chest height inside the car, take a deep breath and push the door open to swim out.
8. Swim straight up toward the surface, following air bubbles, and climb onto the roof if you can.

title: Floodwater rising into the house
quickSummary: Cut the main power at once and move upstairs with your survival kit.
steps: 1. SWITCH OFF THE MAIN BREAKER and shut off the gas as soon as water reaches the door sill.
2. Quickly pack your phone, power bank, flashlight, drinking water, medicine, and ID into a waterproof bag.
3. Move older adults and young children to the second floor or the highest loft.
4. Bring tools to break through the roof (hammer, crowbar, pliers) in case water covers the loft ceiling and you must escape onto the roof.
5. Put on life jackets, or tie empty plastic jerrycans together as makeshift floats.
6. Hang or wave a bright red or yellow cloth from the roof and call 112 with your location.

title: House fire and thick smoke
quickSummary: Stay low, crawl along the floor, and cover your nose and mouth with a wet cloth as you escape.
steps: 1. Shout "FIRE! FIRE!" to warn everyone and sound the alarm.
2. Soak a cloth, mask, or shirt and cover your nose and mouth tightly.
3. CROUCH OR CRAWL ALONG THE FLOOR. Cleaner, cooler air stays in the lowest 30–50 cm.
4. Feel the door handle with the back of your hand before opening it. If it is BURNING HOT, do NOT open the door.
5. If the exit is blocked, go into a room with an outside window and seal the door gaps with wet cloth so toxic smoke cannot pour in.
6. Open the window for fresh air, wave a bright cloth, and call 114 with the floor and room where you are trapped.
7. Never hide under a bed, in a wardrobe, or in a sealed bathroom.

title: Severe lightning nearby
quickSummary: Stay away from tall trees and power poles. Crouch with your feet together.
steps: 1. If your hair stands up or your skin tingles, lightning is about to strike very close.
2. CROUCH AT ONCE. Make yourself as small as possible: feet pressed together, head on your knees, hands over your ears.
3. TOUCH THE GROUND ONLY WITH THE BALLS OF YOUR FEET, to limit step voltage through the heart.
4. NEVER lie flat on the ground.
5. Drop metal objects (hoe, shovel, fishing rod, steel-ribbed umbrella) at least 5 meters away.
6. Stay away from lone trees, ponds, rivers, streams, and open metal structures.
7. If you are in a car, stay inside with the windows closed. The metal body acts as a Faraday cage.

title: Landslide risk on a hillside
quickSummary: Run sideways across the slope. Do not run downhill with the mudflow.
steps: 1. If you hear an unusual roar or loud cracking, or see the slope start to move, DROP YOUR BELONGINGS AND RUN.
2. DIRECTION: run at a right angle to either SIDE of the slope. Never run downhill along a stream bed.
3. Stay out of narrow valleys and drainage gullies.
4. If you cannot get clear, shelter behind a large mature tree or a solid natural boulder.
5. Curl into a ball and lock your arms over your head, neck, and chest.

title: Severe bleeding
quickSummary: Press hard and continuously on the wound with gauze or a clean cloth. Do not let go.
steps: 1. Call 115 at once, or ask someone nearby to call.
2. Press sterile gauze or a clean cloth straight down on the wound with firm pressure.
3. KEEP PRESSURE ON for at least 10–15 minutes. Do not lift the gauze to look, or the clot may break.
4. If blood soaks through, add a new layer on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first layer.
5. Raise the injured arm or leg above the heart unless you suspect a fracture.
6. If blood spurts (a severed artery) and direct pressure fails, consider a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound, toward the heart, and write down the time it was applied.

title: Someone is drowning
quickSummary: Throw a float. Do not jump in unless you are trained in deep-water rescue.
steps: 1. Shout loudly so more people come to help.
2. RESCUE FROM SHORE FIRST. Throw a swim float, an empty plastic jerrycan on a rope, a long branch, or a rope, then pull the person in.
3. Do not jump in unless you are a trained water rescuer. A panicking person can pull you under.
4. Once they are ashore, lay them on their back on a firm, dry surface.
5. If they are unconscious and NOT breathing normally, start CPR chest compressions at once (100–120 per minute).
6. Do NOT carry them upside down and run in circles. That wastes the minutes needed for CPR.

title: Unconscious or not breathing (CPR)
quickSummary: Call 115 and compress the chest continuously at 100–120 times per minute.
steps: 1. Check for a response: tap both shoulders and shout "Can you hear me?"
2. Check breathing for 5–10 seconds by watching the chest rise and fall.
3. If they are not breathing, or only gasping, put the phone on speaker and call 115.
4. Place the heel of one hand on the center of the lower half of the breastbone and lace the other hand on top.
5. PUSH HARD AND FAST: 5–6 cm deep, at 100–120 beats per minute (the rhythm of "Stayin' Alive").
6. Let the chest recoil fully after each compression.
7. Keep going without stopping until medical help arrives or the person starts breathing again.

title: Venomous snakebite
quickSummary: Keep the bitten limb still and below the heart, and get to a hospital that stocks antivenom.
steps: 1. Move out of the snake's striking range. Note its color and head shape, or photograph it from a safe distance.
2. Have the person LIE STILL. Movement spreads venom into the blood faster.
3. Remove rings, watches, bracelets, shoes, and socks from the bitten limb before it swells.
4. Gently wash the wound with saline or clean water.
5. Splint the bitten limb with a board or stick and keep it lower than the heart.
6. If you suspect a neurotoxic snake such as a krait or king cobra, apply a pressure bandage from below the bite upward.
7. Go at once to the nearest hospital that has snake antivenom.

title: Electric shock and live wires in water
quickSummary: Cut the power first. Separate the person with a non-conductive object. Do not touch them with bare hands.
steps: 1. DO NOT TOUCH the person until the power is off.
2. Switch off the main breaker, unplug the cord, or trip the breaker at once.
3. If you cannot cut the power, stand on a dry insulator (dry wood or a rubber mat) and use a dry bamboo or wooden pole, or a plastic broom, to knock the wire off the person.
4. If floodwater is live, do not wade in. Stay at least 10 meters away and call the power utility emergency line.
5. Once they are clear of the current, check breathing. If they are not breathing, start CPR at once and call 115.
